prize_parts.citation: For the development of sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry, reversible-terminator fluorescent nucleotides on clonally amplified surface clusters, that made massively parallel DNA sequencing possible

statement.case_for: Having read the full first round, I still regard massively parallel sequencing (B017) as the only game-changer on the shortlist that is both a new chemical capability and fully demonstrated: reversible-terminator nucleotides, fluorescent readout and clustered single-molecule templates turned a chemical reaction into a digital measurement, and two decades of use across genomics, diagnostics and cancer and infectious-disease monitoring leave no maturity question. Five of eight members now name it in their preferred configuration, from enzymology, biophysical chemistry, simulation and materials viewpoints, so this is not one subfield's taste. I have changed my preferred configuration: I withdraw Pascal Mayer from the third seat and now propose Balasubramanian and Klenerman alone. The clustered-template chemistry stays in the citation, because it is part of the Solexa chemistry the pair built, but I cannot put a third name on it when the priority record is not verified.
statement.case_against: Sequencing already had a Chemistry prize in 1980, and a sceptic can read this as scaling a recognised capability and as a tool for biology and medicine. The citation must therefore say plainly that the recognised discovery is the chemistry of reversible-terminator nucleotides and surface-bound templates. A two-name prize also leaves out Mayer, Ju and Rothberg, who have real claims, and the 454 pyrosequencing and semiconductor lineage is not recognised at all. I accept that cost; a precise two-name attribution that the record supports is better than a third name that rests on my background knowledge. If the committee cannot accept B017, B048 is my fallback, with the cleanest attribution of the remaining candidates.

responses.point: Andrei keeps the Cambridge pair and says he cannot verify the priority split between Solexa and the earlier Mayer/Mosaic work from the material provided.
responses.response: This is what moved me. In round 1 I defended Mayer on the strength of the clonal-colony concept, but neither of us can show from the committee material that his idea was decisive for the platform that actually carried the field. The citation can name clonally amplified clusters without a third laureate, and I now agree with Andrei that the pair is the defensible core. If expert reports later show the cluster concept was independent and decisive, I would reopen the third seat, but I will not vote for it on assertion.

responses.point: Heiner, as chair, now ranks B017 first and proposes Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Mayer, with Mayer credited for the clustered colony-array concept, and he asks whether the wording can avoid arbitrarily excluding the pyrosequencing and semiconductor routes.
responses.response: I supported that three-name set in round 1 and I am stepping back from it. On the wording problem, I think a citation naming reversible-terminator sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry on clustered templates is narrower and more honest than 'massively parallel sequencing' alone, since it says why Ju and Rothberg are not in the configuration: the claim is for one chemical route and its integration, not for the field. The 454 lineage is a loss I would state openly in the committee record rather than hide behind broad wording.

responses.point: Daniel prefers the two-person award and would not oppose Mayer only if expert reports show the cluster idea was decisive, and he wants the citation to state that the discovery is chemistry rather than medicine.
responses.response: We now agree on the laureate set and on the condition for reopening it. I also take his point on the chemistry-versus-medicine objection and have put the nucleotide and surface chemistry into the citation. Where I differ is that I do not want a second part such as B052 added: the lack of an approved degrader drug and the eight-name credit list make it too immature for me, and by my own standard it has not yet shown its consequences.

responses.point: Peter B. adds a second part, nitrogenase structure credited to Douglas Rees alone, beside the B017 pair, and admits the two topics have no obvious joint motivation.
responses.response: I respect the structural work and Rees's crystallography is clearly the load-bearing step, but I do not support the second part. A Rees-only citation drops Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe, whose genetic, mechanistic and cofactor results are central, and the N2 binding mechanism is still debated, so the story is incomplete. Two unrelated parts also look like a compromise, and B017 stands as a complete prize on its own.

responses.point: Peter S. prefers Buchwald and Hartwig C-N coupling alone, and answers the chair that the problem is distinct from the 2010 C-C prize.
responses.response: His case for clean two-person attribution is strong and it is why B048 is my fallback. The Kosugi tin-amide work was a precedent but not the general catalytic method, so I do not think it forces a third name. I still rank B048 below B017 because the reach of sequencing across the field is much greater and its core chemistry has not been honoured before; I do not see his 2010 objection as disqualifying, but it makes me hesitate.

uncertainties: Whether expert reports would show Mayer's clonal-cluster idea was independent and decisive, which would reopen the third seat.
Whether the committee accepts sequencing by synthesis as new chemistry rather than an extension of the work recognised in 1980.
Whether the Cambridge pair alone is accepted by the members who preferred other first choices (Somfai, Sparr, Zou).
My knowledge of the priority claims among the sequencing groups is background knowledge and is not independently verified from the committee material.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the shortlisted candidates. My Warshel/EVB and Uppsala biomolecular simulation background is related to B037, but I have no personal or institutional tie to its candidates and do not support it. No recusal is needed.
